fatal_errors: The proposed sluggish-diffusion, entropy-stabilized mechanism is the opposite of the target mechanism, in which active diffusion and surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation govern stability.

It predicts retention of a homogeneous solid solution up to 1923 K, whereas the target reports instability above approximately 673 K, Au/Cu surface enrichment, melting or evaporation, and a 22% size reduction by 973 K.
The hypothesis is generic and does not reconstruct the equiatomic sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral nanoparticles.
The proposed experiment omits the target vacuum heating protocol, discrete temperature steps, heating rate, microscopy time constraint, and shape- and size-dependent analysis.
No genuine controlled comparison is specified; references to lower-entropy or defect-rich systems are not implemented as matched experimental arms.
The cited evidence concerns different alloy compositions and supports stability only up to approximately 873–1000 K, so it cannot justify homogeneous stability across 473–1923 K.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of thermal stability in multimetal nanoparticles and supplies measurable endpoints and a falsification rule, but it reconstructs neither the material-specific intervention nor the observed governing mechanism. The hidden target challenges the conventional high-entropy/sluggish-diffusion expectation: Au and Cu diffuse to the surface because of surface-energy differences, with reshaping enhancing diffusion and eventual melting or evaporation. The generated hypothesis instead adopts that conventional expectation as its central claim. Its baseline characterization is usable, and XRD, STEM-EDS, atom-probe, and diffusion measurements could detect instability, but the experiment lacks a matched control and the decisive correlation among Au/Cu surface enrichment, self-diffusivity, particle shape, and particle loss. Evidence E2 and E3 establishes that some other HEA or MEA nanoparticles can remain stable at lower temperatures, not that the proposed mechanism applies universally or persists to 1923 K; E3 even notes evaporation under microscope vacuum. Thus the hypothesis is testable but insufficiently supported and directly contrary to the target result.
